title: Keyword Co-occurance Analysis
text:
I use keyword co-occurrence analysis to examine the substantive organization of the SMU-affiliated corpus. The method belongs to the same broad family of bibliometric techniques as co-citation and co-author analysis, but its object is different: rather than asking which authors collaborate or which publications are cited together, it asks which research keywords co-occur across a collection of publications. Authors and databases use keywords to characterize the content of a publication, typically identifying concepts, topics, methods, populations, objects of study, or research problems. The underlying assumption is that these keywords are not distributed randomly. When two keywords repeatedly appear together in the same publications, that recurrence provides evidence that the ideas are being brought into relation within the literature. Co-word analysis therefore allows me to move from a collection of individual publications to a representation of the substantive relationships that recur across the corpus, without beginning from a predetermined classification of the literature.
A keyword co-occurrence network is constructed by first counting these relationships. In the simplified example, a co-occurrence matrix contains six research keywords in its rows and columns, with each intersecting cell recording how many times a pair of keywords appears together. Sport and Identity, for example, have a co-occurrence value of five, whereas Identity and Network Analysis co-occur only once.

The matrix is then converted into an undirected, weighted network using methods of network analysis. Each keyword becomes a node, and an edge connects two nodes when the corresponding keywords occur together in at least one publication. The weight of the edge records the frequency of that co-occurrence, allowing more recurrent relationships to be represented by thicker lines.
Once represented as a network, additional measures can be used to describe the position of individual keywords and the structure of the network as a whole. Degree records the number of other keywords to which a keyword is directly connected, so a high-degree keyword is more extensively embedded in the network than one with relatively few connections. Clustering algorithms such as Louvain identify groups of keywords that are more densely connected to one another than to the rest of the network.
Example Keyword Co-Occurrence Network
In the toy example, Masculinity, Sport, and Identity form one such group, while Network Analysis, Bibliometrics, and Data Science form another. The strongest relationships include Network Analysis–Bibliometrics (6), Sport–Identity (5), and Bibliometrics–Data Science (5). By contrast, the single co-occurrence between Identity and Network Analysis creates a comparatively weak bridge between the two clusters. The visualization therefore makes both internal cohesion and cross-cluster connection visible. Spatial position should be interpreted cautiously, however, because it is partly a consequence of the layout algorithm rather than an independent substantive property.
What the resulting network reveals is not simply which keywords are common, but how the substantive vocabulary of a research corpus is organized relationally. Nodes identify the concepts present in the literature; degree indicates how broadly those concepts are connected; edge weights show which associations recur more or less frequently; and clusters identify concentrations of keywords that repeatedly occur together. When the highly connected keywords within a cluster point toward a coherent substantive concern, those clusters can reasonably be interpreted as research areas or thematic formations. The network can also identify bridging concepts that connect otherwise distinct areas of research and more peripheral keywords that occupy specialized positions.

title: Keyword Co-occurance Analysis
text:
The SMU-affiliated keyword network
In what follows, I use keyword co-occurrence analysis to map recurring intellectual associations within the SMU-affiliated corpus of 7,850 publications. The network focuses on how the keywords used to describe those publications are connected. Groups of densely connected keywords are represented as clusters, but these clusters should not be understood as predetermined departments, disciplines, or administrative categories. They are emergent groupings of concepts, research problems, methods, populations, and objects of study that recur together across the corpus. The resulting network therefore provides a way of examining both what SMU-affiliated researchers study and how different areas of research are related within the indexed literature.
A connection between two keywords indicates that the keywords have been used together in describing the same scholarly output; it does not imply that they have the same meaning or necessarily belong to the same discipline. What matters analytically is the pattern of relationships among keywords. A keyword may be highly connected because it appears alongside many different topics, while another may occupy a more specialized position because its connections are concentrated within a narrower area of research. The network is therefore best understood as a map of research association and connectedness rather than simply a count of topics.
The network combines two forms of keyword metadata. Author keywords are keywords selected by authors to describe the subject matter of their publications, while database-generated keywords, such as Keywords Plus, are derived from information in the bibliographic record to identify additional topical relationships. These were combined before constructing the network to provide a broader representation of the subjects and concepts associated with each publication. As a result, a node labelled migration, galaxies, or education represents a keyword in the bibliographic description of the corpus, not a researcher, department, publication, or project.
The vocabulary itself is heterogeneous. Some keywords identify broad substantive areas, while others refer to theoretical concepts, research methods, populations, geographic locations, objects of study, scientific processes, or highly specialized phenomena. Because author-supplied and database-generated keywords are combined, the network should be interpreted as a representation of how SMU research is bibliographically described and connected, rather than as a direct inventory of the concepts researchers themselves would necessarily identify as most important.

title: Keyword Co-occurance Analysis
section: How to use the network and tables
text:
How to use the network and tables
The interactive network provides the broadest view of these relationships. Use the keyword search above the network to locate a particular keyword. Selecting a keyword highlights its node in yellow with a black border. Once selected, the nodes connected directly to that keyword are also highlighted. The network can then be zoomed and panned to bring these linked nodes into focus, and individual nodes may be dragged to make crowded areas easier to inspect. Moving a node changes only its position on the screen and does not alter the underlying network analysis.
When you look at a keyword together with all of its neighbours, you are looking at that keyword’s immediate local network. The selected keyword is the focal keyword, and each neighbour is another keyword that appeared with it in the metadata of at least one publication in the corpus. The neighbourhood therefore shows the set of topics, concepts, methods, populations, places, or objects of study that have been directly associated with that keyword in SMU-affiliated research. This neighbourhood can be interpreted as a picture of the keyword’s intellectual context. A keyword with neighbours drawn largely from its own cluster is embedded mainly within a relatively concentrated area of research. Selecting the keywords “behaviour”, “radial velocities”, “health”, “management history”, or “actor network theory” from the keyword drop down search menu offers an illustration of this type of pattern. A keyword whose neighbours span several clusters may instead connect otherwise distinct areas of scholarly activity. Selecting the keywords “origin”, “sequence”, or “evolution” will illustrate this type of pattern.
Nodes with the same colour belong to the same intellectual cluster.1 Node size represents degree of connectedness: larger nodes are directly connected to a greater number of other keywords in the network, while smaller nodes have fewer direct connections and tend to occupy more specialized positions. Node size therefore represents network connectedness rather than the quality, importance, or volume of research associated with a keyword.
The tables provide complementary ways of examining the same network.

The Keyword neighbours table allows a reader to select an exact keyword and retrieve all of the keywords directly connected to it, ordered by the strength of their co-occurrence. This value is a measure of how often the focal keyword and a particular neighbour appear together in the publication metadata. For example, searching for the keyword “health” in this table reveals that “health” and “canada” co-occur 9 times in this dataset.
The Cluster profiles table provides a compact overview of the vocabulary associated with each intellectual cluster.
The Cluster vocabulary table lists every keyword in the network by cluster, allowing readers to move beyond the most prominent keywords and examine more specialized areas that may be difficult to identify visually.
The Author lookup table will return the titles of publications of an author. This presented partly as a means of allowing those interested to think through and assess the coverage of the WoS database.

The Cluster profiles and Cluster vocabulary look up tables provide insight into the structure of these clusters. The tables report each keyword’s rank and degree.2

On this basis of the above, what begins to emerge is that the SMU-affiliated research corpus contains 7 research clusters whose “identities” have yet to be specified.
In the same way that the all the keywords used in the SMU-affiliated corpus can be arranged in a network and “decomposed” into 7 clusters, each of these 7 clusters can be explored in the same way. “Decomposing” these research clusters allows for their structure to be explored more carefully, opening up an opportunity to think more clearly about what each of these 7 research clusters is “about”–and what this might say about the university as a whole.
At the top of the page, you’ll find links to details about each of the 7 research clusters. Currently, only data for Clusters 1 and 7 are available. In the spirit of “member checking” (Birt et al. 2016; McKim 2023), I invite you to review these details. Does this data resonate with your understanding of your own scholarly activity and/or the activity at SMU?

title: Work, governance, and well-being
text:
Cluster 2 brings together research on how organizations and institutions make decisions, and how the conditions they create shape people’s opportunities, experiences, and health. That thread is clearest in the two communities that study employment. Personnel selection research examines how employers judge applicants, how applicants manage the impressions they make, and whether interview ratings predict job performance. The workplace stress and leadership community takes up what happens once people are at work. Its focus is on how supervision, job demands, and social support relate to burnout, safety, job satisfaction, and turnover.
The corporate governance community shifts the focus from employees to firms. Its research asks who oversees firms, what information firms disclose, and how investors assess their performance. The gender and inequality community also examines organizations and labour markets, with a different question about outcomes. It asks how access to work, earnings, and participation vary across social groups. Its work on identity, religion, and belonging extends that inquiry beyond employment. The environmental governance community takes questions about authority and participation into another setting. Where corporate governance concerns oversight of firms, environmental governance concerns how institutions and communities share decisions about resources, protect ecosystems, and respond to climate risks that can affect livelihoods unevenly.
The public health community shares the workplace community’s interest in health and the conditions that shape it. Its focus is on how common physical activity, smoking, and alcohol use are among youth and adults, and how factors such as barriers to activity and exposure to advertising enter into the research. Taken together, the six communities give the cluster a focus on work, governance, inequality, and health. Their connections are clearest where they ask who makes decisions, what information those decisions draw on, and how the consequences are distributed.
Below are two forms of information that together help characterize what the smaller keyword communities within this research cluster are “about.” The first is a word cloud in which each keyword’s font size reflects its within-community PageRank. PageRank measures a keyword’s structural prominence by considering both the strength of its connections and the prominence of the keywords connected to it. Because these scores depend on one another, the calculation accounts for connections across the entire community. Keywords shown in larger font therefore have greater structural prominence within that community. The second is a list of publications strongly affiliated with the community. Together, the word cloud and the affiliated publications offer a window into the research activity represented by the keyword network.

















The first community in Cluster 2 centres on how employers assess job applicants and how applicants present themselves during selection. “Behavior,” “model,” and “personality” have the highest within-community PageRank, while “employment interview,” “impression management,” and “applicant faking” give those terms a more specific context. The keywords point to questions about what interview ratings capture, how reliably they predict job performance, and how applicants respond to formats such as asynchronous video interviews.
A second strand concerns the psychology of sexual offending, with terms such as “pedophilia,” “hebephilia,” “offenders,” and “recidivism.” Personnel selection is the clearest focus for the community heading, with sexual offending as a distinct topic within the same keyword grouping.












Community 2 of Cluster 2 centres on how firms are governed, what information they disclose, and how these practices relate to performance. “Performance” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.080), followed by “impact” (0.050) and “information” (0.044). “Corporate governance,” “ownership,” “boards,” and “agency costs” point to questions about how firms are overseen and whose interests guide their decisions. “Voluntary disclosure,” “earnings management,” and “information asymmetry” point to what investors can learn about a firm and how reliably they can assess it. Other terms, such as “investment,” “innovation,” and “corporate social responsibility,” broaden the focus to the choices firms make and their consequences for performance and reputation. The connection with Community 1 is the problem of assessing performance from information that others help shape. In Community 1, employers assess applicants who manage the impressions they make in interviews. In Community 2, investors assess firms that make choices about what to disclose and how to report their earnings.












Community 3 of Cluster 2 centres on how gender shapes people’s experiences in organizations, labour markets, families, and public life. “Gender” (0.059), “Canada” (0.052), and “women” (0.048) have the highest within-community PageRank, with the United States also appearing as a setting. “Discrimination,” “earnings,” and “participation” point to questions about access and economic outcomes, while “race,” “sexual orientation,” and “intersectionality” broaden the inquiry to how different forms of inequality overlap. A strand on religiosity, secularity, and moral boundaries examines how people define belonging and difference. The closest connection to Community 1 is through employment. That community examines how employers assess applicants, while this one asks how opportunities and rewards are distributed across social groups. The connection to Community 2 runs through organizations and power. Corporate governance research asks who oversees firms and whose interests guide decisions. Here, the emphasis is on how gender and other social distinctions shape who participates and on what terms.












Community 4 of Cluster 2 focuses on how people and institutions manage ecosystems and respond to environmental change. “Management” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.042), followed by “conservation” (0.025), “climate-change” (0.024), “governance” (0.022), and “adaptation” (0.022). One strand concerns biodiversity, restoration, and the protection of species and habitats. Another examines how people adapt to climate change, with “vulnerability,” “migration,” and “livelihoods” pointing to the consequences for coastal communities. Fisheries co-management brings the two strands together by raising questions about how decisions over a resource are shared among the people and institutions that depend on or manage it. This extends Community 2’s interest in who makes decisions from firms to environmental governance. It also connects to Community 3’s work on inequality through questions about whose livelihoods are exposed to environmental change and who has the resources or authority to respond.












This community in Cluster 2 examines how working conditions and supervision shape employee health, safety, and attachment to the organization. “Work” (0.044), “stress” (0.034), and “transformational leadership” (0.031) have the highest within-community PageRank. Keywords such as “job demands,” “incivility,” and “abusive supervision” point to sources of strain, while “social support,” “trust,” and “organizational justice” point to conditions that can shape how employees experience work. The outcomes range from burnout and psychological distress to job satisfaction, turnover, and injuries. Terms such as “intervention,” “training,” and “prevention” bring in the question of what organizations can do to improve working conditions. The connection to Community 1 is through employment. That community examines how applicants are assessed at entry, while this one examines what happens once people are at work. It also connects to Community 3 through questions of fairness, here with an emphasis on how employees are treated in their day-to-day working lives.












This community in Cluster 2 focuses on how common health-related behaviours are and what shapes them. “Youth” (0.054) and “prevalence” (0.049) have the highest within-community PageRank, with “physical activity,” “alcohol,” and “smoking” identifying the main areas of study. “Adolescents” and “adults” indicate that the research spans age groups. “Time use,” “compendium,” and “barriers” point to how researchers measure physical activity and examine what limits participation. “Tobacco,” “substance use,” “images,” and “advertising” point to a second strand on substance use and the media environments in which it occurs. The community shares an interest in health with the workplace stress community. Here the emphasis is on how behaviours are distributed across age groups and what shapes them in everyday life.

text:
The expansion of corporate management models within higher education over the past several decades has begun to change how academic knowledge is produced, evaluated, and incentivised. To greater and lesser degrees, universities have transitioned away from traditional collegial governance structures toward managerial frameworks, commonly known as New Public Management (NPM). Under this corporate paradigm, senior university administration relies on institutional strategic research plans, formal performance indicators, and centralised accountability metrics to align faculty behaviours with broader organisational objectives.
Below, I review some recent scholarship on academic managerialism to contextualise what for me, is becoming an increasinly intersting question: do strategic research plans work?

The expansion of corporate management models within higher education over the past several decades has begun to change how academic knowledge is produced, evaluated, and incentivised. To greater and lesser degrees, universities have transitioned away from traditional collegial governance structures toward managerial frameworks, commonly known as New Public Management (NPM). Under this corporate paradigm, senior university administration relies on institutional strategic research plans, formal performance indicators, and centralised accountability metrics to align faculty behaviours with broader organisational objectives.
Below, I review some recent scholarship on academic managerialism to contextualise what for me, is becoming an increasinly intersting question: do strategic research plans work?

title: Describing the SMU-affiliated Research Corpus
text:
Academic Managerialism
The introduction of corporate steering in public research sectors is frequently framed as a necessary mechanism to increase operational efficiency and institutional accountability. Scholars examining the Central and Eastern European contexts demonstrate that department heads are forced to act as primary mediators, negotiating the friction between emerging corporate managerial expectations and traditional academic autonomy (Machovcova, Zabrodska, and Mudrak 2019). This transition shifts the university from an open site of unconstrained intellectual inquiry to a managed environment where output is being both quantified and regularised. Empirical observations of these policy shifts suggest that while they aim to stimulate public research efficiency, they can function as a double-edged sword, leading to administrative inflation and narrow publishing strategies among faculty (Schubert 2009).
The global reach of these corporate practices is evident across diverse higher education landscapes, including developing regions such as the United Arab Emirates, where new managerialism is deployed to reshape institutional reputations (Ajayan and Balasubramanian 2020). When fiscal cutbacks occur, the pressure to maintain research performance becomes even more acute; institutions are forced to sustain or accelerate output levels even when financial incentives and direct support is declines (Bak and Kim 2023). At the core of this management system is the corporate premise that academic institutions are structurally no different from any commercial enterprise and can therefore be optimised through auditing and performance-monitoring systems (Hasham 2018). Consequently, the historical evolution of research performance measurement systems, particularly within heavily evaluated sectors like Australian higher education, outlines a steady intensification of administrative oversight (Martin-Sardesai et al. 2019).

title: Describing the SMU-affiliated Research Corpus
section: Institutional Leadership and Strategic Shared Visions
text:
Institutional Leadership and Strategic Shared Visions
A central tenet of corporate strategic planning is that institutional leadership is in a position to steer research excellence. Recent quantitative modeling of presidential capabilities in Chinese higher education argues that specific strategic competencies at the executive level correlate positively with institutional performance gains and international visibility (Dong, Wu, and Yu 2025). Similarly, evaluations of academic leadership and university performance across European and Russian contexts investigate whether universities demonstrate measurable improvements when led by active, highly cited scholars who embody research excellence, rather than pure career administrators (Gerashchenko 2022). This structural steering is frequently reinforced by regional contagion effects, where the strategic choices and performance trajectories of neighbouring peer institutions create a normative pressure that drives local academic leadership to adopt identical strategic management models (Saftiuc, Proscanu, and Teodorescu 2025).
For these administrative plans to translate into scholarly output, university leaders direct attention to building an institutional shared vision that attempts to bridge the historical divide between research and teaching mandates (Bui et al. 2024). Senior management relies on transformational leadership styles, operating under the assumption that inspiring a collective corporate identity will foster internal creativity and outputs (Salim and Zakaria 2021). In fields such as green innovation and technology transfer, evidence indicates that the specific academic and corporate experiences of the top management team can shape the volume and direction of institutional innovation outputs (Zhao et al. 2021). Moreover, when academic executives retain active boardroom connections, they can connect lab-based research with high-impact industrial commercialisation, demonstrating how top-down strategies attempt to steer basic science toward applied economic utility (Zhu, Wu, and Gaidai 2025).

title: Describing the SMU-affiliated Research Corpus
text:
Guiding Research Productivity
At the level of the faculty member, the primary mechanisms used to enforce strategic alignment are institutional incentives, formal performance appraisals, and individual research productivity tracking. Evidence suggests that while structured interventions can alter short-term output counts, they rarely change long-term scholarly trajectories (Ryazanova and Jaskiene 2022). While routine bibliometric reports are frequently positioned as one tool among many, these data summaries often function as coercive monitoring mechanisms that hold individual faculty accountable to generic performance targets (Cabezas-Clavijo and Torres-Salinas 2021). In some cases, advanced institutional frameworks have emerged, such as bibliometric strength, potential, and risk analysis models, which allow administrators to track exactly how faculty publication choices respond to central strategic choices and funding pathways (Iping et al. 2024).
The efficacy of these incentive structures remains dependent on localized professional contexts and personal scholarly investments. In Canada, broad empirical studies of primary care researchers demonstrate that productivity is strongly associated with protected research time, dedicated infrastructure, and targeted team-based funding rather than purely top-down corporate mandates (Aggarwal et al. 2024). Furthermore, the specialized nature of research production is heavily reliant on specific cognitive resources and long-term personal investments, which means that arbitrary administrative redirections can result in cognitive friction and operational inefficiency for the scholar (Degli Antoni, Fia, and Sacconi 2022). Quantitative analyses of individual academic research agendas confirm that broader organizational factors and institutional priorities interact directly with disciplinary traditions, meaning that top-down steering tools must constantly compete with an academic’s internalized scholarly values and peer networks (Horta and Santos 2020).

title: Describing the SMU-affiliated Research Corpus
text:
Tensions, Resistance, and Academic Freedom
The imposition of corporate performance management has generated tensions, with many scholars arguing that these frameworks stifle academic freedom and distort genuine knowledge production. Critical discourse analyses highlight that aggressive performance management frameworks force a precarious state of affairs upon academic work, transforming scholarly writing into a rushed commodity designed to satisfy auditing cycles rather than solve profound intellectual problems (Morrish and Sauntson 2016). This shift creates a sense of alienation, where academic identities are systematically reconfigured to fit the parameters of the managed university, sparking widespread subtle resistance among faculty who seek to protect their professional autonomy from neoliberal encroachment (Morrish 2017). In specialized fields like social work education, the imposition of a marketized, neo-liberal agenda is shown to directly compromise the critical, social-justice mission of the discipline by prioritizing commercial metric capture over community engagement (MacDonald and Nixon 2016).
The human cost of these auditing regimes is captured in qualitative terms by academics who describe the modern pressure cooker environment (Xu and Poole 2024). This creates institutional struggles for recognition where individual departments are pitted against one another for scarce resources, fragmenting the university’s traditional community of scholars (Muench and Baier 2012). Moreover, the formal policies and administrative structures often lack meaningful faculty buy-in because they are perceived as top-down compliance exercises rather than authentic scholarly transformations (Castro-Gomez et al. 2026). Without aligning internal policy incentives directly with the intrinsic motivations and professional values of the faculty, centralized administrative mandates fail to cultivate genuine participation or sustainable scholarly growth (Barsallo et al. 2026).

title: Describing the SMU-affiliated Research Corpus
text:
Do Strategic Research Plans Work?
This breief review on higher education management demonstrates a conflict between top-down corporate steering and bottom-up faculty behaviour. While institutional theories and administrative models posit that clear leadership capabilities, shared corporate visions, and targeted bibliometric monitoring can successfully optimize and direct an institution’s research performance, empirical accounts expose resistance, strategic gaming, and profound alignment failures. This contradiction exposes a gap in evaluative scientometrics: we lack robust, objective, longitudinal measures of whether corporate university strategies genuinely shape the intellectual landscape of an institution or if they merely retroactively rebrand pre-existing, faculty-driven strengths.
It is with this in mind that I raise the following question: do strategic research plans work?
I explore this question turning to the research corpus of Saint Mary’s University (SMU).

title: Describing the SMU-affiliated Research Corpus
text:
Data
This bibliometric study examines 36 years of SMU-affiliated research, from January 1990 through December 2025. The corpus is restricted to publications for which the institutional affiliation metadata explicitly identifies SMU. No restrictions were placed on document type. These deliberately broad parameters were intended to capture the full range of scholarly outputs indexed by Web of Science (WoS) that can be attributed to faculty, staff, and researchers associated with SMU, providing a basis for examining publication behaviour, research activity, and patterns of connection and collaboration across the university community over the period.
The search produced a corpus of 7,850 publications appearing across 2,862 different publication sources, reflecting a wide range of scholarly venues and the disciplinary breadth of the university. The corpus should not, however, be treated as a complete inventory of everything produced at SMU. Web of Science is widely used for bibliometric research, but, like all bibliographic databases, it is selective. Its coverage tends to favour English-language journals and disciplines in which journal articles and collaborative publication are dominant forms of scholarly communication. Fields in which research is more often communicated through books, book chapters, regional journals, professional publications, or other locally oriented venues may therefore be less completely represented. This is particularly consequential for some areas of the humanities and social sciences. The analysis should accordingly be understood as a description of the SMU research activity visible through Web of Science rather than an exhaustive account of the university’s entire research culture.

title: Evolution
text:
“Evolution” serves as reasonable umbrella for much of the material in Research Cluster 1 because its communities draw attention to how the things they study came to be and how they changed over time. Across these communities, a major through line is the use of evidence available today to reconstruct a history.
Questions of galaxy formation capture the first community. Its keywords trace how clouds of gas collapse, how young stars gather material from surrounding disks, and how stellar oscillations help researchers probe the structure of stars as they evolve. A secondary thread in this community focuses on evolution via sexual selection and population formation.
Geological considerations account for six of the nine keyword communities. Across these communities, researchers use rocks, minerals, and sediments to reconstruct how geological systems formed and changed. In Atlantic Canada, that work spans the assembly of the northern Appalachians and the history of offshore basins, where sandstones preserve evidence of where sediments came from and what happened after burial. Work in southern Mexico uses rock ages and deformation to reconstruct ancient plate boundaries, while research in northwest China examines both continental growth and basin development. The volcanic-rock geochemistry community follows the origins of magmas across tectonic settings, and the British Columbia community brings that interest in magmatic processes to questions about ore formation.
One keyword network points to questions about biological lineages and how they are classified, with a focus on grasses such as wheat, barley, and Elymus. Researchers compare DNA sequences and plant traits to trace ancestry and examine how interbreeding and changes in chromosome number have shaped relationships among lineages. Arabidopsis’ role as a plant model adds further support in suggesting that this community hinges on questions about plant biology more generally.
A separate community examines discrimination and the economic and social lives of sexual and gender minorities. Its keywords point to research on earnings and self-employment among gay men, lesbians, and same-sex couples, alongside questions about gender identity, inclusion, and mental health. Its presence in the cluster captures a distinct line of research on how people are treated and how they fare in markets and other social settings.
Below are two forms of information that together help characterize what the smaller keyword communities within this research cluster are “about.” The first is a word cloud in which each keyword’s font size reflects its within-community PageRank. PageRank measures a keyword’s structural prominence by considering both the strength of its connections and the prominence of the keywords connected to it. Because these scores depend on one another, the calculation accounts for connections across the entire community. Keywords shown in larger font therefore have greater structural prominence within that community. The second is a list of publications strongly affiliated with the community. Together, the word cloud and the affiliated publications offer a window into the research activity represented by the keyword network.

















I read this community as centred on how stars form and change over time. “Evolution” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.145), and the terms that follow it give the community an astrophysical focus. Hydrodynamic models, interstellar clouds, collapse, and accretion trace the formation of stars from clouds of gas and dust, while protostars and protoplanetary disks point to the early stages of stellar and planetary development. Research on stellar oscillations and metallicity extends that focus to the structure and evolution of stars.
I also see a strand of research in which evolution takes on a biological meaning, with a focus on sexual selection and population structure. Kinship, pairwise relatedness, and gene flow point to questions about how populations are structured. Research on sexual selection includes how body size and sexual size dimorphism relate to mating success, as well as how traits such as physical attractiveness and social cues such as reputation figure in mate preferences.












I read this community as research that uses the chemistry of rocks to reconstruct where magmas came from and how they changed before eruption. “Geochemistry” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.068), followed by “volcanic-rocks” and “petrogenesis,” the study of how rocks form. Trace elements and neodymium and strontium isotopes provide clues to the sources of magmas and to processes such as crystallization, mixing, and interaction with the continental crust. The tectonic terms give these questions a setting, from subduction and island arcs to continental rifting and volcanism associated with mantle plumes. Studies from the Canadian Cordillera, the Aegean, and the Himalaya–Tibet region show how this line of inquiry plays out across different geological settings.












I read this community as giving the cluster’s geological research a Maritime and northern Appalachian focus. Nova Scotia has the highest within-community PageRank (0.081), followed by New Brunswick, the Maritimes Basin, and the northern Appalachians. Where the geochemistry community studies how volcanic rocks form across a range of tectonic settings, this community uses geochemistry, uranium–lead dating, and petrology to reconstruct the history of a particular region. Studies of the South Mountain Batholith and the Cobequid Highlands bring that history into view at the scale of individual rock bodies and field areas, while work on sedimentary basins and terrane boundaries traces how the region took shape.












I read this community as a focus on the molecular evolution and classification of plant life, centred on grasses. “Origin” (0.055) and “classification” (0.052) have the highest within-community PageRank, followed by “Triticeae” and “Poaceae.” “Origin” in this context is most reasonably understood as “evolutionary ancestry”. The prominence of wheat, Hordeum, and Elymus gives the research a focus within the grass family. Arabidopsis, as a model plant used in biology, supports the suggestion that this community centres on plant biology. Keywords such as “RPB2 gene,” “chloroplast genome,” and “morphology” point to the evidence researchers use to reconstruct ancestry. Introgression, polyploidy, and multiple origins point to why those histories can be difficult to classify. This community develops a biological strand of the earlier evolution community by bringing questions of lineage and classification to the foreground. Alongside the geochemistry and Maritime geology communities, it adds another kind of historical reconstruction to the cluster, using genes and plant traits to trace how lineages formed.












I read this community as extending the cluster’s Maritime geological focus offshore, with an emphasis on where sediments came from and what happened to them after deposition. “Provenance” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.050), and the prominence of “offshore Nova Scotia,” “margin,” “sandstones,” and “basin” places that question on the eastern Canadian continental margin, particularly in the Scotian Basin. Stratigraphy and depositional facies point to how sediments accumulated, while diagenesis and thermal history point to how burial, heating, and fluid movement altered the resulting rocks. The closest overlap is with the Maritime and northern Appalachian community, which also studies basin development alongside granite emplacement and terrane assembly. The contrast with the geochemistry community is in what “origin” means: there the question is how magmas formed, while here it is where sediment grains came from and what they can tell us about the history of a basin.












This community adds a focus on discrimination and economic life to the cluster. “Discrimination” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.182), followed by “gay men,” “sexual orientation,” and “lesbians.” The prominence of “same-sex,” “couples,” “self-employment,” and “earnings” gives that focus a labour-market dimension, with questions about how individuals and couples make a living and how their economic outcomes differ. “Gender identity,” “inclusion,” and “mental health” extend the discussion to how people are treated and how they fare beyond earnings. The earlier evolution community also included research on sex differences and mate preferences. Here, sexuality figures in a different set of questions, about how social institutions and markets shape the lives of sexual and gender minorities.












This community adds a focus on how the rocks of southern Mexico record the movement of continents and the history of ancient oceans. “Geochronology” (0.063) has the highest within-community PageRank, followed by “Acatlán Complex” (0.061) and “Mexico” (0.055). The Acatlán and Oaxacan complexes give the research a regional anchor, while “Laurentia,” “Gondwana,” “Rheic Ocean,” and “Pangea” point to questions about where these blocks of crust once lay and how they came together. Dating establishes the sequence of events, while deformation and high-pressure metamorphism provide clues to how rocks were buried, transformed, and brought back toward the surface. The closest parallel is the Maritime and northern Appalachian community, which also uses rock ages and terrane relationships to reconstruct tectonic history. Here, the emphasis is on using a regional rock record to work out the former positions of continents and the oceans between them.












This community gives the cluster’s geological research a focus on continental growth and basin development in northwest China. “West Junggar” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.081), followed by “Sr–Nd” (0.073) and “continental growth” (0.070). Strontium and neodymium isotopes connect this community to the earlier work on volcanic-rock geochemistry. Here, “orogenic belt,” “remnant ocean basin,” and “ophiolitic mélange” place that evidence in the context of how continental crust grew as ocean basins closed. That question parallels the reconstruction of ancient plate boundaries in the southern Mexico community. The keywords also point to work on the Junggar Basin itself, where “Mahu Sag,” “rift basin,” “Fengcheng Formation,” and “provenance analysis” bring basin development, sediment sources, and past environments into view. This strand bears some resonance with Scotian Basin (check this) community, where sedimentary rocks also provide a record of how a basin developed.












This community brings ore formation to the foreground of the cluster’s geological research, with British Columbia as its named setting. All eight keywords have the same within-community PageRank , so the focus comes from reading them together. “Gold deposit,” “porphyry,” and “platinum-group elements” identify the kinds of deposits and metals under study, while “magmatic-hydrothermal fluids” and “ore genesis” point to questions about how fluids associated with magmas transport and concentrate metals. This overlaps with the volcanic-rock geochemistry community’s interest in magmatic processes and with the Maritime community’s work on mineralization, including the Kemptville tin deposit. Here, the question of how an ore deposit forms is the focus of the community.

title: Evolution
text:
I read this community as centred on how stars form and change over time. “Evolution” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.145), and the terms that follow it give the community an astrophysical focus. Hydrodynamic models, interstellar clouds, collapse, and accretion trace the formation of stars from clouds of gas and dust, while protostars and protoplanetary disks point to the early stages of stellar and planetary development. Research on stellar oscillations and metallicity extends that focus to the structure and evolution of stars.
I also see a strand of research in which evolution takes on a biological meaning, with a focus on sexual selection and population structure. Kinship, pairwise relatedness, and gene flow point to questions about how populations are structured. Research on sexual selection includes how body size and sexual size dimorphism relate to mating success, as well as how traits such as physical attractiveness and social cues such as reputation figure in mate preferences.

title: Evolution
text: I read this community as research that uses the chemistry of rocks to reconstruct where magmas came from and how they changed before eruption. “Geochemistry” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.068), followed by “volcanic-rocks” and “petrogenesis,” the study of how rocks form. Trace elements and neodymium and strontium isotopes provide clues to the sources of magmas and to processes such as crystallization, mixing, and interaction with the continental crust. The tectonic terms give these questions a setting, from subduction and island arcs to continental rifting and volcanism associated with mantle plumes. Studies from the Canadian Cordillera, the Aegean, and the Himalaya–Tibet region show how this line of inquiry plays out across different geological settings.

title: Evolution
text: I read this community as giving the cluster’s geological research a Maritime and northern Appalachian focus. Nova Scotia has the highest within-community PageRank (0.081), followed by New Brunswick, the Maritimes Basin, and the northern Appalachians. Where the geochemistry community studies how volcanic rocks form across a range of tectonic settings, this community uses geochemistry, uranium–lead dating, and petrology to reconstruct the history of a particular region. Studies of the South Mountain Batholith and the Cobequid Highlands bring that history into view at the scale of individual rock bodies and field areas, while work on sedimentary basins and terrane boundaries traces how the region took shape.

title: Evolution
text: I read this community as a focus on the molecular evolution and classification of plant life, centred on grasses. “Origin” (0.055) and “classification” (0.052) have the highest within-community PageRank, followed by “Triticeae” and “Poaceae.” “Origin” in this context is most reasonably understood as “evolutionary ancestry”. The prominence of wheat, Hordeum, and Elymus gives the research a focus within the grass family. Arabidopsis, as a model plant used in biology, supports the suggestion that this community centres on plant biology. Keywords such as “RPB2 gene,” “chloroplast genome,” and “morphology” point to the evidence researchers use to reconstruct ancestry. Introgression, polyploidy, and multiple origins point to why those histories can be difficult to classify. This community develops a biological strand of the earlier evolution community by bringing questions of lineage and classification to the foreground. Alongside the geochemistry and Maritime geology communities, it adds another kind of historical reconstruction to the cluster, using genes and plant traits to trace how lineages formed.

title: Evolution
text: I read this community as extending the cluster’s Maritime geological focus offshore, with an emphasis on where sediments came from and what happened to them after deposition. “Provenance” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.050), and the prominence of “offshore Nova Scotia,” “margin,” “sandstones,” and “basin” places that question on the eastern Canadian continental margin, particularly in the Scotian Basin. Stratigraphy and depositional facies point to how sediments accumulated, while diagenesis and thermal history point to how burial, heating, and fluid movement altered the resulting rocks. The closest overlap is with the Maritime and northern Appalachian community, which also studies basin development alongside granite emplacement and terrane assembly. The contrast with the geochemistry community is in what “origin” means: there the question is how magmas formed, while here it is where sediment grains came from and what they can tell us about the history of a basin.

text: This community adds a focus on discrimination and economic life to the cluster. “Discrimination” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.182), followed by “gay men,” “sexual orientation,” and “lesbians.” The prominence of “same-sex,” “couples,” “self-employment,” and “earnings” gives that focus a labour-market dimension, with questions about how individuals and couples make a living and how their economic outcomes differ. “Gender identity,” “inclusion,” and “mental health” extend the discussion to how people are treated and how they fare beyond earnings. The earlier evolution community also included research on sex differences and mate preferences. Here, sexuality figures in a different set of questions, about how social institutions and markets shape the lives of sexual and gender minorities.

text: This community adds a focus on how the rocks of southern Mexico record the movement of continents and the history of ancient oceans. “Geochronology” (0.063) has the highest within-community PageRank, followed by “Acatlán Complex” (0.061) and “Mexico” (0.055). The Acatlán and Oaxacan complexes give the research a regional anchor, while “Laurentia,” “Gondwana,” “Rheic Ocean,” and “Pangea” point to questions about where these blocks of crust once lay and how they came together. Dating establishes the sequence of events, while deformation and high-pressure metamorphism provide clues to how rocks were buried, transformed, and brought back toward the surface. The closest parallel is the Maritime and northern Appalachian community, which also uses rock ages and terrane relationships to reconstruct tectonic history. Here, the emphasis is on using a regional rock record to work out the former positions of continents and the oceans between them.

Strontium and neodymium isotopes connect this community to the earlier work on volcanic-rock geochemistry. Here, “orogenic belt,” “remnant ocean basin,” and “ophiolitic mélange” place that evidence in the context of how continental crust grew as ocean basins closed. That question parallels the reconstruction of ancient plate boundaries in the southern Mexico community. The keywords also point to work on the Junggar Basin itself, where “Mahu Sag,” “rift basin,” “Fengcheng Formation,” and “provenance analysis” bring basin development, sediment sources, and past environments into view. This strand bears some resonance with Scotian Basin (check this) community, where sedimentary rocks also provide a record of how a basin developed.

Cluster 7 centres on how compounds are made, how their atoms are arranged, and how that arrangement affects their reactivity. The coordination and organometallic chemistry community studies how ligands bind to metals and uses X-ray crystallography to characterize the resulting complexes. The chemical reactivity community examines how compounds behave and how their bonds change. Keywords such as “basicity,” “radicals,” and “adducts” show the breadth of that inquiry. Catalysis is one strand within it, with “oxidative addition” and “reductive elimination” pointing to steps in reactions involving metal complexes. Other communities give these questions a more specific focus through palladium cross-coupling, polymerization, and amination. Work on indium extends the cluster’s interest in bonding and reactivity to main-group chemistry, where redox-active ligands can participate in electron transfer.
Structural characterization also connects communities that study different kinds of materials. The ionic liquids and dyes community includes work on the composition and electrochemical behaviour of liquid salts, alongside research on boron dyes. The molecular recognition community uses diffraction to study how hydrogen bonds organize molecules into networks in solids. Across these communities, structure matters at different scales, from the arrangement of atoms around a metal to the ways molecules interact and assemble.
The cluster also contains an engineering community focused on designing and operating renewable energy systems. Its keywords concern how wind and solar generation, storage, and control can be combined, with cost and environmental impact among the criteria for evaluating designs. “Feedback” and “dispatch” suggest a related interest in operating decisions, although those two terms leave the application open.
Below are two forms of information that together help characterize what the smaller keyword communities within this research cluster are “about.” The first is a word cloud in which each keyword’s font size reflects its within-community PageRank. PageRank measures a keyword’s structural prominence by considering both the strength of its connections and the prominence of the keywords connected to it. Because these scores depend on one another, the calculation accounts for connections across the entire community. Keywords shown in larger font therefore have greater structural prominence within that community. The second is a list of publications strongly affiliated with the community. Together, the word cloud and the affiliated publications offer a window into the research activity represented by the keyword network.

















The first community in the Chemistry cluster centres on how metal complexes are made, how their atoms are arranged, and how they react. “Chemistry” (0.086), “complexes” (0.081), and “derivatives” (0.070) lead the PageRank ranking, while “coordination,” “transition-metal complexes,” and the names of metals such as osmium, tungsten, and palladium give the community a more specific focus. “Crystal-structures” and “X-ray crystallography” point to work on how ligands bind to metal centres, while “insertion” and “substitution” point to reactions that change those complexes. This community overlaps with Cluster 2’s work on molecular structure and chemical reactivity. What gives it a focus of its own is that metal complexes are the objects being synthesized, characterized, and modified.












The second community in Cluster 2 centres on how atoms are arranged in crystals and molecules and how researchers determine those arrangements. “Crystal-structure” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.086), followed by “ab initio” (0.049) and “molecular-structure” (0.039). The keywords bring together computational approaches, such as molecular orbital calculations, and experimental methods, such as diffraction and Raman spectroscopy. Terms like “symmetry,” “conformations,” and “vibrational spectrum” show what these methods help characterize. Hydration, dehydration, and hydrolysis point to a related interest in how compounds interact with water and change in its presence or as it is removed. This community gives Cluster 2 a focus in structural and computational chemistry alongside the first community’s work on personnel selection and applicant assessment.












The third community in Cluster 2 centres on how renewable energy systems are designed and operated. “System” (0.077) and “design” (0.071) have the highest within-community PageRank, followed by “optimization” (0.031). Keywords such as “wind energy,” “solar photovoltaic,” “microgrid,” and “battery” point to research on combining power generation and storage, while “energy management” and “control” concern how those systems operate. “Cost” and “environmental impacts” indicate criteria for evaluating design choices, and “desalination” points to an application beyond electricity supply. Alongside personnel selection and structural chemistry, this community adds an engineering focus to Cluster 2.












This community in Cluster 7 examines how compounds react and how their bonds break and form. “Reactivity” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.103), more than three times that of “reduction” (0.029), the next-ranked term. Keywords such as “basicity,” “adducts,” and “radicals” show the breadth of the work. Catalysis is one strand within it, with “hydroboration,” “hydrogenation,” and “olefin metathesis” naming reactions under study and “oxidative addition” and “reductive elimination” pointing to individual reaction steps. The clearest overlap is with Cluster 7’s coordination and organometallic chemistry community. Both examine how metal complexes react, with this community giving more attention to the steps by which chemical transformations occur.












The fifth community in Cluster 2 centres on the design and characterization of metal complexes, with atomic layer deposition as a prominent application. “Ligands” (0.047), “crystal” (0.046), “atomic layer deposition” (0.042), and “cobalt” (0.040) have the highest within-community PageRank. “Precursor,” “amides,” and “thermal analysis” point to research on how compounds are prepared and evaluated for use in depositing thin films. The emphasis on ligands and molecular structure overlaps with the crystal and molecular structure community, while “hydrosilylation” connects this grouping to the earlier work on chemical reactivity and catalysis. A separate strand, marked by “tuberculosis,” “lipophilic,” and “antimicrobial,” points to research on compounds with potential antimicrobial activity.












The sixth community in Cluster 2 centres on cholinesterases and how compounds interact with them. “Acetylcholinesterase” and “butyrylcholinesterase” share the highest within-community PageRank (0.041), followed by “mechanism” (0.037). Keywords such as “docking,” “analogs,” and “substrate” point to research on how molecules bind to or act on these enzymes. “Alzheimer’s disease” and “amyloid plaques” give the community a biomedical focus, while “exposure,” “toxicity,” and “cells” suggest work on how compounds affect cells. The emphasis on molecular structure and reaction mechanisms connects this community to the earlier chemistry communities, here in the context of biological activity and disease.












Community 7 of the Chemistry cluster brings together research on ligands, positively charged compounds, and catalysis. “Ligand” (0.057) and “cations” (0.056) have the highest within-community PageRank, followed by “Lewis acids” and “dications” (both 0.049). These terms point to questions about how compounds bind and how charge affects their bonding and reactivity. “Phosphine,” “pincer complexes,” and “crystal structures” connect the community to the cluster’s work on the structure of metal complexes, while “palladium” and “cross-coupling reactions” give it a link to the chemical reactivity and catalysis community. What distinguishes this grouping is the emphasis on ligands and charge as ways to understand how compounds bind and react.












Community 8 focuses on the structure of transition-metal complexes and their roles in catalysis and polymerization. “X-ray structure” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.109), followed by “asymmetric catalysis” and “tantalum” (both about 0.058). “Metal-carbon bonds,” “niobium,” and “titanocene” give the structural work an organometallic focus, while “olefin polymerization” and “opening metathesis polymerization” point to research on how metal complexes help build polymer chains. The use of X-ray methods connects this community to Community 1’s work on the structure of metal complexes, and the metathesis terms connect it to the chemical reactivity community. Community 7 foregrounds ligands, charge, and palladium cross-coupling. Here, the catalytic keywords emphasize polymer formation and reactions that favour one mirror-image form of a product over the other.












Community 9 brings together work on ionic liquids, boron dyes, and metal complexes. “Crystal structure” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.064), followed by “boron” (0.044) and “ionic liquids” (0.043). “Salts,” “room-temperature melts,” “tetrachloroaluminate,” and “electrochemistry” point to research on the composition and behaviour of ionic liquids, while “BODIPY dyes” and “azadipyrromethenes” point to a strand of dye chemistry. The emphasis on structural characterization connects this community to Community 1’s work on coordination compounds and Community 8’s use of X-ray structure. “Palladium(II)” and “N-heterocyclic carbene” also overlap with the cluster’s work on metal complexes and chemical reactivity. Ionic liquids and dyes give Community 9 its own focus within that broader chemistry.












Community 10 focuses on how molecules recognize one another and assemble into structures in the solid state. “Molecular recognition” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.084), followed by “hydrogen-bond” (0.074), “acid” (0.072), and “solid-state” (0.072). Together with “network” and “supramolecular chemistry,” these terms point to research on how hydrogen bonds between molecules help organize them into extended structures. “Second-harmonic generation” also points to an interest in the optical properties of solids. X-ray diffraction connects this community to the structural work in Communities 1, 8, and 9. What distinguishes Community 10 is its emphasis on interactions between molecules and the patterns those interactions produce in a solid.












This community focuses on amination, the introduction of an amino group into a compound. “Amination” (0.101), “bromides” (0.095), and “amines” (0.084) have the highest within-community PageRank. Together with “(hetero)aryl chlorides,” they point to research on forming carbon–nitrogen bonds using amines and halide substrates. The closest connection is to Community 7’s work on cross-coupling and to the broader chemical reactivity community. This grouping gives that work a specific synthetic focus in how to form carbon–nitrogen bonds.












This community focuses on the structure and reactivity of main-group compounds, with indium as the named example. “X-ray diffraction” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.075), followed by “indium,” “main-group elements,” and “redox-active ligands” (each 0.068). Diffraction connects this work to Communities 1 and 8, which also use crystal structures to characterize compounds. The emphasis here shifts from transition-metal complexes to main-group chemistry. Community 7 offers another point of comparison. Both communities examine the role of ligands, but here the emphasis is on ligands that can themselves gain or lose electrons during a reaction. “Efficient synthesis” and “organic-synthesis” point to an interest in using that reactivity to make compounds.












“Feedback” and “dispatch” have effectively equal within-community PageRank (0.067). Read together, they suggest an interest in how operating decisions are adjusted as conditions change. The closest thematic parallel in Cluster 7 is Community 3’s work on renewable energy systems, where feedback can inform when to generate power or draw on storage.

title: Chemistry
text: The first community in the Chemistry cluster centres on how metal complexes are made, how their atoms are arranged, and how they react. “Chemistry” (0.086), “complexes” (0.081), and “derivatives” (0.070) lead the PageRank ranking, while “coordination,” “transition-metal complexes,” and the names of metals such as osmium, tungsten, and palladium give the community a more specific focus. “Crystal-structures” and “X-ray crystallography” point to work on how ligands bind to metal centres, while “insertion” and “substitution” point to reactions that change those complexes. This community overlaps with Cluster 2’s work on molecular structure and chemical reactivity. What gives it a focus of its own is that metal complexes are the objects being synthesized, characterized, and modified.

title: Chemistry
text: The second community in Cluster 2 centres on how atoms are arranged in crystals and molecules and how researchers determine those arrangements. “Crystal-structure” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.086), followed by “ab initio” (0.049) and “molecular-structure” (0.039). The keywords bring together computational approaches, such as molecular orbital calculations, and experimental methods, such as diffraction and Raman spectroscopy. Terms like “symmetry,” “conformations,” and “vibrational spectrum” show what these methods help characterize. Hydration, dehydration, and hydrolysis point to a related interest in how compounds interact with water and change in its presence or as it is removed. This community gives Cluster 2 a focus in structural and computational chemistry alongside the first community’s work on personnel selection and applicant assessment.

title: Chemistry
text: The third community in Cluster 2 centres on how renewable energy systems are designed and operated. “System” (0.077) and “design” (0.071) have the highest within-community PageRank, followed by “optimization” (0.031). Keywords such as “wind energy,” “solar photovoltaic,” “microgrid,” and “battery” point to research on combining power generation and storage, while “energy management” and “control” concern how those systems operate. “Cost” and “environmental impacts” indicate criteria for evaluating design choices, and “desalination” points to an application beyond electricity supply. Alongside personnel selection and structural chemistry, this community adds an engineering focus to Cluster 2.

title: Chemistry
text: This community in Cluster 7 examines how compounds react and how their bonds break and form. “Reactivity” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.103), more than three times that of “reduction” (0.029), the next-ranked term. Keywords such as “basicity,” “adducts,” and “radicals” show the breadth of the work. Catalysis is one strand within it, with “hydroboration,” “hydrogenation,” and “olefin metathesis” naming reactions under study and “oxidative addition” and “reductive elimination” pointing to individual reaction steps. The clearest overlap is with Cluster 7’s coordination and organometallic chemistry community. Both examine how metal complexes react, with this community giving more attention to the steps by which chemical transformations occur.

title: Chemistry
text: The fifth community in Cluster 2 centres on the design and characterization of metal complexes, with atomic layer deposition as a prominent application. “Ligands” (0.047), “crystal” (0.046), “atomic layer deposition” (0.042), and “cobalt” (0.040) have the highest within-community PageRank. “Precursor,” “amides,” and “thermal analysis” point to research on how compounds are prepared and evaluated for use in depositing thin films. The emphasis on ligands and molecular structure overlaps with the crystal and molecular structure community, while “hydrosilylation” connects this grouping to the earlier work on chemical reactivity and catalysis. A separate strand, marked by “tuberculosis,” “lipophilic,” and “antimicrobial,” points to research on compounds with potential antimicrobial activity.

title: Chemistry
text: The sixth community in Cluster 2 centres on cholinesterases and how compounds interact with them. “Acetylcholinesterase” and “butyrylcholinesterase” share the highest within-community PageRank (0.041), followed by “mechanism” (0.037). Keywords such as “docking,” “analogs,” and “substrate” point to research on how molecules bind to or act on these enzymes. “Alzheimer’s disease” and “amyloid plaques” give the community a biomedical focus, while “exposure,” “toxicity,” and “cells” suggest work on how compounds affect cells. The emphasis on molecular structure and reaction mechanisms connects this community to the earlier chemistry communities, here in the context of biological activity and disease.

title: Chemistry
text: Community 7 of the Chemistry cluster brings together research on ligands, positively charged compounds, and catalysis. “Ligand” (0.057) and “cations” (0.056) have the highest within-community PageRank, followed by “Lewis acids” and “dications” (both 0.049). These terms point to questions about how compounds bind and how charge affects their bonding and reactivity. “Phosphine,” “pincer complexes,” and “crystal structures” connect the community to the cluster’s work on the structure of metal complexes, while “palladium” and “cross-coupling reactions” give it a link to the chemical reactivity and catalysis community. What distinguishes this grouping is the emphasis on ligands and charge as ways to understand how compounds bind and react.

title: Chemistry
text: Community 8 focuses on the structure of transition-metal complexes and their roles in catalysis and polymerization. “X-ray structure” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.109), followed by “asymmetric catalysis” and “tantalum” (both about 0.058). “Metal-carbon bonds,” “niobium,” and “titanocene” give the structural work an organometallic focus, while “olefin polymerization” and “opening metathesis polymerization” point to research on how metal complexes help build polymer chains. The use of X-ray methods connects this community to Community 1’s work on the structure of metal complexes, and the metathesis terms connect it to the chemical reactivity community. Community 7 foregrounds ligands, charge, and palladium cross-coupling. Here, the catalytic keywords emphasize polymer formation and reactions that favour one mirror-image form of a product over the other.

title: Chemistry
text: Community 9 brings together work on ionic liquids, boron dyes, and metal complexes. “Crystal structure” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.064), followed by “boron” (0.044) and “ionic liquids” (0.043). “Salts,” “room-temperature melts,” “tetrachloroaluminate,” and “electrochemistry” point to research on the composition and behaviour of ionic liquids, while “BODIPY dyes” and “azadipyrromethenes” point to a strand of dye chemistry. The emphasis on structural characterization connects this community to Community 1’s work on coordination compounds and Community 8’s use of X-ray structure. “Palladium(II)” and “N-heterocyclic carbene” also overlap with the cluster’s work on metal complexes and chemical reactivity. Ionic liquids and dyes give Community 9 its own focus within that broader chemistry.

title: Chemistry
text: Community 10 focuses on how molecules recognize one another and assemble into structures in the solid state. “Molecular recognition” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.084), followed by “hydrogen-bond” (0.074), “acid” (0.072), and “solid-state” (0.072). Together with “network” and “supramolecular chemistry,” these terms point to research on how hydrogen bonds between molecules help organize them into extended structures. “Second-harmonic generation” also points to an interest in the optical properties of solids. X-ray diffraction connects this community to the structural work in Communities 1, 8, and 9. What distinguishes Community 10 is its emphasis on interactions between molecules and the patterns those interactions produce in a solid.

title: Chemistry
text: This community focuses on amination, the introduction of an amino group into a compound. “Amination” (0.101), “bromides” (0.095), and “amines” (0.084) have the highest within-community PageRank. Together with “(hetero)aryl chlorides,” they point to research on forming carbon–nitrogen bonds using amines and halide substrates. The closest connection is to Community 7’s work on cross-coupling and to the broader chemical reactivity community. This grouping gives that work a specific synthetic focus in how to form carbon–nitrogen bonds.

title: Chemistry
text: This community focuses on the structure and reactivity of main-group compounds, with indium as the named example. “X-ray diffraction” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.075), followed by “indium,” “main-group elements,” and “redox-active ligands” (each 0.068). Diffraction connects this work to Communities 1 and 8, which also use crystal structures to characterize compounds. The emphasis here shifts from transition-metal complexes to main-group chemistry. Community 7 offers another point of comparison. Both communities examine the role of ligands, but here the emphasis is on ligands that can themselves gain or lose electrons during a reaction. “Efficient synthesis” and “organic-synthesis” point to an interest in using that reactivity to make compounds.

The closest thematic parallel in Cluster 7 is Community 3’s work on renewable energy systems, where feedback can inform when to generate power or draw on storage.
